intro: ICMR recommends a Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) of 0.83g of protein per kilogram of body weight per day for a healthy, sedentary Indian adult - meaning a 60kg adult needs roughly 50g daily.
If you're strength training or physically active, sports nutrition research supports 1.2-1.6g/kg, meaningfully higher than the baseline RDA.

Protein requirements aren't one-size-fits-all, and most generic "how much protein do you need" content online quotes Western guidelines that don't reflect Indian dietary research. Here's what India's own official guidance actually says, how it changes based on your activity level, and just as important - what it doesn't recommend.

sections.heading: What ICMR's official RDA actually says?
paragraphs: The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), through the National Institute of Nutrition (NIN), sets India's official nutrient guidelines. The 2020 ICMR-NIN guidelines set the Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) at 0.66g/kg/day and the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) at 0.83g/kg/day for a healthy, sedentary adult - meaning a 60kg adult needs approximately 50g of protein daily to meet baseline requirements.

sections.heading: Why active individuals typically need more?
paragraphs: ICMR's RDA is calculated as a minimum to prevent deficiency in a sedentary population - it isn't designed as an optimal target for someone strength training or otherwise physically active.

Sports nutrition research, including the International Society of Sports Nutrition's position stand, supports higher intakes of 1.2-1.6g/kg/day for individuals engaged in regular resistance training or muscle-building goals - a meaningfully higher target than the baseline RDA.

proteinTable.heading: Daily Protein Needs by Activity Level

cautionSection.heading: What India's dietary guidelines actually caution about supplements?
cautionSection.label: Important, and often left out of supplement-brand content
paragraphs: India's 2024 ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines specifically caution against relying on protein powder supplements for muscle building, citing potential risks - including bone mineral loss and kidney concerns - associated with prolonged, high-dose intake of protein powders or concentrates. The guidance emphasizes meeting protein needs primarily through food, with quality protein sources like pulses, dairy, and lean meats forming the foundation of intake.

We think it matters to say this plainly, even as a supplement brand: a protein powder is meant to fill a genuine gap in your daily intake - not replace whole food as your primary protein source. If you're consistently falling short of your target through food alone, a quality protein supplement can help close that gap; it isn't a substitute for a balanced diet.

expertSection.heading: Dt. Chirag Pandey's perspective
expertSection.quote: The biggest mistake I see is people either ignoring protein entirely or over-relying on powder to hit an arbitrary number. Start with your actual food intake, identify the real gap, and use a supplement to close it - not replace it. Most people are surprised how much protein they're already getting from dal, dairy, and everyday meals once they actually track it.
expertSection.author: Dt. Chirag Pandey, Registered Dietitian & Co-Founder, Gomzi Supplement

calculatorSection.heading: A simple way to calculate your own target
paragraphs: Multiply your body weight in kg by your activity-level factor from the table above.
For example, a 70kg moderately active adult: 70 × 1.1 (midpoint of 1.0-1.2) ≈ 77g of protein per day.
Track your actual food intake for a few days before assuming you need a large supplement dose - most people are closer to their target than they expect.
calculatorSection.formula: Daily protein target = Body weight (kg) × Activity-level factor

faqs.question: Is the ICMR RDA enough if I go to the gym regularly?
faqs.answer: For most people doing regular strength training, the baseline ICMR RDA of 0.83g/kg is likely insufficient - sports nutrition research supports 1.2-1.6g/kg for this activity level.

faqs.question: Can I get enough protein from an Indian vegetarian diet alone?
faqs.answer: Yes, with planning - combining pulses, dairy, and other quality plant protein sources can meet even elevated protein targets, though it typically requires more deliberate meal planning than a mixed diet.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take whey protein daily?
faqs.answer: For most healthy adults, moderate daily use as part of a balanced diet is considered safe - but sustained very high intake is where caution is warranted, per the ICMR-NIN guidance above. If you have any kidney or health concerns, consult a doctor or dietitian before increasing protein intake significantly.

faqs.question: Do older adults need more or less protein?
faqs.answer: More, not less - ICMR-NIN guidance for adults 60+ recommends higher intake (around 54g/day for men, 45.7g/day for women, before activity adjustment) to help prevent age-related muscle loss (sarcopenia).

bottomLine.heading: The bottom line
paragraphs: Most people significantly overestimate or underestimate their real protein needs because they're working from generic, non-Indian guidelines or marketing claims rather than official data.

Start with ICMR's baseline RDA, adjust upward based on your real activity level, prioritize food first, and use a quality protein supplement to close genuine gaps - not as a default replacement for whole food.

intro: A quick note before you read on: This article shares general nutrition information, not medical advice. GLP-1 medications should only be started, adjusted, or stopped under a doctor's guidance. Speak to your physician or a registered dietitian about your specific treatment plan and protein needs.

At Gomzi Supplement, we've noticed a pattern in the last year: more and more customers writing in to say they're on a GLP-1 weight-loss plan, eating far less than before, and worried they're losing muscle along with the fat. They're not imagining it.

GLP-1 medications (the semaglutide class of drugs, often referred to by brand names like Ozempic or Wegovy) have become one of the most talked-about weight-management tools in India through 2025–2026. They work by suppressing appetite - which means less food overall, and for many people, that means less protein too. And when total protein intake drops while you're in a calorie deficit, your body doesn't just burn fat. It burns muscle.

This guide explains why that happens, how much protein you likely need to protect your muscle while on a GLP-1 plan, and practical ways to close that gap - including where a protein supplement fits in.

sections.heading: Why GLP-1 weight loss comes with a muscle-loss risk?
paragraphs: Research tracking body composition changes in people on GLP-1 medications has found that a meaningful share of total weight lost is lean mass, not just fat - in some studies, lean mass has accounted for a notable proportion of overall weight loss.

This isn't unique to GLP-1 drugs; it happens with any aggressive calorie deficit. But because GLP-1 medications suppress appetite so effectively, people often eat far below their protein needs without realizing it, which accelerates the problem.

Muscle isn't just about how you look. It's active tissue that supports your metabolism, blood sugar regulation, strength, and mobility - losing too much of it while losing weight can undermine the very health outcomes the weight loss was meant to achieve.

sections.heading: How much protein do you actually need?
paragraphs: General nutrition guidance for adults trying to preserve muscle during a calorie deficit typically points toward a higher protein intake than the standard baseline recommendation - closer to 1.2–1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day for most active adults, though your exact needs depend on your weight, activity level, and medical situation.
This is general information, not a personalized target - your doctor or a registered dietitian can help you calculate what's right for you.

The practical challenge on a GLP-1 plan is volume: if your appetite is significantly suppressed, hitting that protein number through food alone - three eggs, a chicken breast, a bowl of dal - can be genuinely difficult when you simply don't feel hungry enough to eat that much.

sections.heading: Closing the protein gap without forcing extra food
paragraphs: Prioritize protein first at every meal - eat your protein source before anything else on the plate while your appetite allows it.
Spread protein across the day in smaller amounts rather than one large meal, since appetite suppression can make big meals harder to finish.

Use a protein supplement to fill the gap on days when food alone doesn't get you there - this is often the simplest lever, since a single scoop can deliver 20–25g of protein in a small volume that's easy to consume even with reduced appetite.
Pair protein intake with light resistance training where possible - even 2–3 short sessions a week signals your body to preserve muscle rather than break it down.

sections.heading: Where a protein supplement fits in?
paragraphs: This is exactly the situation whey protein was built for: getting meaningful protein into your body without needing to eat a large volume of food. A scoop of Gomzi Supplement whey protein delivers a concentrated dose of protein in a small, easy-to-consume serving - useful when your appetite is suppressed but your protein needs haven't gone down.
Explore our whey protein range to find a flavor and format that fits into a lower-appetite routine.

faqs.question: Does whey protein interfere with GLP-1 medications?
faqs.answer: There's no established interaction between whey protein and GLP-1 medications for most people, but you should always confirm any new supplement with your doctor, especially alongside prescription treatment.

faqs.question: How much protein should I get from supplements versus food?
faqs.answer: Whole food should still be your primary protein source where your appetite allows. A supplement is best used to close the gap on days when you fall short, not to replace meals entirely.

faqs.question: Will protein powder affect weight loss results?
faqs.answer: Protein itself is calorie-neutral to your weight-loss goal when accounted for in your daily intake - its role here is protecting muscle mass, not adding extra calories beyond what your plan allows.

faqs.question: I'm not on a GLP-1 medication but I'm dieting - does this still apply to me?
faqs.answer: Yes. Anyone in a sustained calorie deficit is at risk of losing muscle along with fat, and higher protein intake plus resistance training is the standard way to protect against it.

bottomLine.heading: The bottom line
paragraphs: If you're on a GLP-1 weight-loss plan, the fat loss is working the way it's meant to - but muscle loss is a real, well-documented side effect that's easy to overlook when your appetite is suppressed.
Prioritizing protein at every meal, and using a supplement like Gomzi Supplement whey protein to fill the gaps, is one of the simplest ways to protect the muscle you've worked to build.
